headline: Agents went always-on; the risk moved to keys and trust
summary: Four labs have shipped always-on agents in about ten weeks, and Walmart will let AI shopping agents onto its site next month while Amazon keeps blocking them. The same week showed the price of that access: Railway disclosed a breach that may have exposed customer API keys, as critical Node.js, PHP2Shell and GitLab patches landed. Leaders are reframing the risk, with Satya Nadella urging companies to treat models as insider risks and OpenAI letting METR and Redwood audit its internal monitoring from the inside. Meanwhile the plumbing is getting cheaper and more standard: DeepSeek open-sourced its inference stack, Agent Skills joined MCP at the Agentic AI Foundation, and the Claude API moved to dated versions. The question for leaders is no longer whether agents can do the work, but whose accounts they hold, under what limits, and how you check what they say they did.

threads.title: Agents go always-on
threads.line: Agents with their own computer are becoming the default product, and big companies are rolling them out to whole workforces.

threads.title: Keys are the attack surface
threads.line: Agent API keys work like credit cards with no fraud checks, and attackers are now going after them.

threads.title: Verify, don't trust
threads.line: Agent reports can overclaim, so oversight moves outside the model: audits, monitoring and checkable evidence.

threads.title: Cheaper, standard plumbing
threads.line: Open inference stacks, shared standards and stable APIs lower switching costs and vendor lock-in.
